title: TfL urged to prioritise investment in escalators
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![General view of a triple escalator at Liverpool Street station. Two are going up and one is going down. Various passengers are standing on all escalators.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/a9e1/live/7a77b300-98ba-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.jpg)
Transport for London must make escalators a funding priority, a Labour London Assembly member has said
- Published
Transport for London (TfL) must spend more to refurbish and replace ageing escalators on the London Underground, a senior London Assembly member has said.
Elly Baker, the transport spokesperson for the City Hall Labour group, said this infrastructure needed to be prioritised to ensure the mayor's active transport targets were feasible.
Freedom of Information data released in July revealed 153 out of 566 escalators â over a quarter â on the Underground were operating beyond their expected shelf life.
TfL has said it works "hard to keep our escalators in good working order, and this includes regular safety checks and a proactive rolling maintenance programme".
![Close-up of Baker who is looking past the camera with a neutral expression. She has short brown hair and hoop earrings.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/470/cpsprodpb/c4f1/live/e7fc5d00-98be-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.png)
Elly Baker, the transport spokesperson for the City Hall Labour group, says escalators must be a top priority
In 2025-26, TfL spent Â£56.1m on escalators, including Â£38.6m of operating expenditure and Â£17.5m of capital expenditure to upgrade, renew and modernise the assets, according to the mayor's office.
In the same period, TfL spent Â£1.3m on "reactive maintenance call-outs for escalators".
Baker said: "It's really important that we make sure escalators are working on the Tube â [but] I am concerned that TfL aren't giving it enough of a priority."
City Hall has a target for 80% of journeys in London to be made by foot, bicycle or public transport by 2041.
Baker said TfL had recently shifted from a model where they would refurbish escalators after 20 years and completely replace them after 40 years to taking a "risk-based approach", where escalators are closely monitored, to save money.
This had led to "more and more escalators going out of service unexpectedly", which in turn, risked putting people off using the network altogether, she argued.
![Broken escalator with missing steps](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c40d/live/df8604f0-98b9-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.jpg)
Last year three out of four escalators at Woolwich Arsenal DLR Station were out of action, including one at the Greens End entrance, which is still broken
A TfL spokesperson said 95% of escalators were available to passengers, "despite heavy usage", adding: "Inevitably, a small number of escalators have had to be temporarily withdrawn from service or are subject to increased maintenance and inspection regimes to ensure they can continue operating with acceptable levels of reliability.
"Funding for replacing these highly complex machines is subject to a prioritisation process which examines assets across the whole TfL network, looking at customer usage and the latest safety and condition assessments."

summary: Transport for London (TfL) must prioritize funding for the refurbishment and replacement of ageing escalators on the London Underground, according to City Hall Labour transport spokesperson Elly Baker. Freedom of Information data shows that over a quarter of the network's escalators are operating beyond their expected shelf life, which Baker argues risks deterring passengers. While TfL maintains that 95% of its escalators are available and subject to regular maintenance, a shift from scheduled replacements to a risk-based approach has led to concerns over unexpected outages.
key_points: Over a quarter of London Underground escalators (153 out of 566) are operating beyond their expected shelf life.
Elly Baker argues that failing to prioritize escalator investment risks undermining active transport targets and putting people off using the network.
TfL has shifted from a fixed-schedule refurbishment and replacement model to a risk-based monitoring approach to save money.
TfL stated that 95% of its escalators remain available for passengers despite heavy usage and a prioritization process for funding across the network.

title: Why is feeding deer in The Royal Parks a problem?
author: Jess Warren
content:
![A sign at Richmond Park telling visitors not to feed the deer.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/3505/live/268038a0-9aed-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
Visitors to London's Royal Parks are being reminded that it is illegal , externalto feed the wild deer after a man was injured by a stag that approached his picnic group.
From safety risks to photographing deer responsibly, here is what you need to know about the deer in Richmond Park and Bushy Park.
Why are people being told not to feed the deer?
Visitors to south-west London's Richmond and Bushy parks are being urged not to feed the red and fallow deer or get within 50m (165ft) of the animals.
On Saturday, a man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag in Richmond Park when it approached his picnic group.
The deer was subsequently shot by a Royal Parks wildlife officer as it was deemed a danger to visitors.
![A black and white image taken in September 1936 of a visitor to Richmond Park reading a Royal Parks notice warning people about "Danger from Deer".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9684/live/e42dcba0-9ae9-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors to Richmond and Bushy parks have been told for decades not to feed the deer
Paul Richards, park manager at Richmond Park, said the animal's behaviour was likely the direct result of having previously been fed by visitors at the park.
"It is only because people had fed this particular animal that its behaviour had changed," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
The "do not feed" warning is not new. The Royal Parks has regularly told people visiting both of the south-west London parks not to feed the wild animals.
How can feeding deer put people at risk?
The deer in both parks are wild animals, and can act unpredictably around humans.
Unlike deer in other places, such as the city of Nara in Japan where deer are regularly fed by people, London's deer should not be approached or fed.
Richards said the deer in The Royal Parks had begun to associate visitors with food, which was "not their natural behaviour".
"Enjoy the deer, respect the deer, keep a safe distance from the deer," he said.
"Don't feed them, they don't need feeding. Some people think they're doing a good deed. In fact you're not, you're doing quite the opposite."
Richards said that if fed, the deer began to associate people with food and would be more likely to approach groups or individuals in the park.
This, he warned, was dangerous to visitors and put them at risk of serious injury.
Feeding deer may also increase the risk of them ingesting plastic, which blocks their stomachs and causes malnutrition.
My children want to pet the deer, why is that not allowed?
Last month, families with young children were seen trying to stroke the deer in Richmond Park.
Richards said his team were "shocked and extremely concerned" by video footage from the park, and called the actions "deeply irresponsible and highly dangerous".
The park manager explained that closing in on the animals would cause the deer stress and risked a "fatal incident".
"Richmond Park's red and fallow deer are wild, powerful animals. Although they may appear calm, they can react suddenly and aggressively if they feel threatened," he said.
"Stags can weigh more than 25 stone (159kg) and run at speeds of up to 30mph (48km/h), making them highly dangerous if visitors get too close."
Do the deer have enough food in the drought?
Red and fallow deer eat grasses, leaves and shoots of trees, as well as acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts.
Richards said: "They don't need to be fed. A lot of people are thinking: 'It's bone dry out there, everything is brown', but the deer don't need supplementary feeding here at Richmond Park."
![A deer reaching up to eat leaves from a tree in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b83e/live/d7565f30-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Deer eat grasses, leaves, acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts
"There's plenty of things for them to eat," he added. "They're grazing on bramble, we're already seeing a bit of an early autumn, and it won't be long before sweet chestnuts are beginning to fall, so there is plenty of food for them."
Visitors are urged not to remove conkers (horse chestnuts) from the park as they are a vital part of the deer's diet and help to build up their fat reserves for winter.
How can I photograph the deer?
London's deer population is much-loved and photographed, due to their apparent juxtaposition with city-life.
The current 630-strong herd of wild red and fallow deer in Richmond Park were first introduced by Charles I in 1637 and roam freely amongst the trees and grasslands.
They have been enjoyed by visitors for decades, but must be respected, Richards said.
![A woman stands beneath a tree to photograph stags in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/869/cpsprodpb/775b/live/64f843e0-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors are told to photograph deer through a zoom lens
"The deer here are wild, they have been here for centuries," he said.
"If you want to photograph them, photograph them using the zoom function on your phone or camera."
He said visitors must keep a distance of 50m (165ft) from the animals.
What should you do if a deer approaches you in a Royal Park?
Visitors are told to never feed or touch the deer in Richmond and Bushy parks.
If one comes towards you, put all food and packaging out of sight and move away slowly and calmly, The Royal Parks says.
People should not try to move the deer away themselves.
"If you witness someone putting themselves, others or the deer at risk, please do not try and intervene but report it immediately to the police," a Royal Parks spokesperson says.

summary: Visitors to London's Richmond and Bushy parks are legally prohibited from feeding the wild deer because it alters their behavior and creates safety risks. A recent incident involving a man injured by a stag led to the animal being shot, highlighting the dangers of approaching or feeding the park's wildlife. Park officials stress that the deer have sufficient natural food sources and urge the public to maintain a distance of at least 50 meters.
key_points: Feeding the wild deer in Richmond and Bushy parks is illegal.
A man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag that approached his picnic group, leading to the animal being shot.
Feeding causes deer to associate humans with food, leading them to approach visitors and increasing the risk of plastic ingestion.
Visitors are advised to keep a distance of 50 meters, avoid petting or feeding the animals, and use zoom lenses for photography.

title: Rain finally falls in London! Capital rejoices as showers hit city with more to come
author: Matt Watts; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![UK: DRONE - London parks dry out amid prolonged heat and lack of rain.](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/e635ba55-b89a-5b3d-ac13-c3a16b31b9f4/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Londoners woke on Tuesday to puddles on the streets, while others celebrated as they heard the rain in the early hours.
The tracker showed rain hitting most of the city - some parts of which haven’t seen any real rain for almost two months.
![Puddles could be seen on streets and pavements in the capital on Tuesday morning](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/5/20/rain-London.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
It comes after England saw the driest July on record - with no meaningful rain in London.
Across the Thames catchment area, just 0.8mm of rain was recorded - a mere 2% of the long-term average.
Many Londoners took to social media to celebrate after the rain fell overnight.
Multiple forecasters are also predicting more rain to fall in the capital in the coming days, with further showers expected later on Tuesday.
Light rain showers are also forecast for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday by BBC weather, and the Met Office is also predicting a chance of showers on those days.
Read More
Most of the showers will fall across parts of north-west England, Northern Ireland and southern Scotland, with some parts of south-east England staying dry.
summary: Rain finally fell in London on Tuesday morning after nearly two months without real rain, following England's driest July on record. Residents celebrated the showers on social media as puddles formed across the city streets. Forecasters predict further rain and light showers for the capital in the coming days.
key_points: London received its first significant rain in nearly two months on Tuesday morning.
England experienced its driest July on record, with London seeing no meaningful rainfall.
Residents celebrated the arrival of the rain on social media.
Forecasters including the Met Office and BBC Weather predict more showers for the capital through the rest of the week.

title: Muslim woman threatened on London bus says abuse is daily
author: Alice Bhandhukravi; Jess Warren
content:
![Salsabil in a blue niqab and headscarf, standing in front of a blue wall.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/924/cpsprodpb/91a3/live/3cce26b0-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.png)
Salsabil says she is regularly abused because of her religious clothing
- Published
A Muslim woman who was abused on a bus in west London for wearing a niqab has said that she is subjected to Islamophobic abuse on a daily basis in the capital.
"Spitting, barging, pushing. It happens to me every single day," says 21-year-old Salsabil.
"We kind of convince ourselves that this is something we have to tolerate rather than report."
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said that "no community in London should have to endure intimidation or abuse" and the force was "committed to tackling all forms of hate crime".
Salsabil said she was travelling home from central London on 31 July when she was verbally abused because of her niqab, a veil for her face that leaves the area around the eyes clear and is worn with a headscarf.
She got off the bus and said she boarded the next one, and was again subjected to verbal abuse regarding her niqab. The incident was captured on video.
"He was swearing at me for the way I'm dressed," Salsabil said.
"I went to go sit down and this passenger stopped me, again, very aggressively, telling me that I'm not welcome with this veil on my face, that this is terrorism, this is not religion.
"He said that if I refuse to take off my veil that he will take it off for me."
Salsabil said the man threatened to kill her, and another passenger intervened and became embroiled in a punch-up with the man.
She said he was the only passenger who came to her defence.
The bus driver intervened and the man was asked to get off, which he did, and Salsabil got off at her normal stop in north-west London.
"I genuinely thought that I was going to be seriously injured," she said. "I felt so alone.
"I'm so grateful for the passenger who did step in and defend me."
'I haven't felt safe in the past year'
She added: "This happens to me really often. If I reported every single incident, I think I would probably just live at the police station."
Salsabil explained that she chose not to report the incident to the Metropolitan Police, after she previously reported an Islamophobic hate crime and officers "were quite dismissive about it".
She said: "A lot of women do report incidents like this and they are dismissed, and being dismissed is very demotivating to ever approach the police again.
"I was born and raised in London and I've always felt safe... but I think recently, for the past year, I haven't felt safe, especially going out on public transport," Salsabil added.
"We should never justify abuse based on how someone dresses," she said. "If a woman chooses to wear the hijab or the niqab, or doesn't choose to wear any religious clothing, she should never feel unsafe."
![A woman holds a smartphone while sitting on a park bench](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/fb42/live/c96d6cd0-9639-11f1-870d-5d08c49babb2.jpg)
The incident on the bus was captured on video and has been seen by the BBC
Siwan Hayward, Transport for London's (TfL) director of security, policing and enforcement, said she was "appalled" by the video of Salsabil being abused on the bus.
"No-one should ever have to fear or experience abuse when using our network," she said.
"We are urgently looking into this incident and encourage anyone who experienced or witnessed this incident to contact the police."
A spokesperson for the Met Police said they were aware of the video and were making efforts to contact the victim, and urged witnesses to report the incident to force.
Both TfL and the Met said they took a zero-tolerance approach to anti-Muslim hatred.
Data collected by the Met Police , externalshowed that reported faith hate crime rose by 25% in London over the past year, and there was a 31% rise in reported Islamophobic offences.
London's victims commissioner, Andrea Simon, said she did not believe Salsabil's experience was a "one-off".
"We have to be very concerned that this is something that's affecting particularly those who might be visibly identifiable by clothing as being Muslim or being of a faith background," she said.
"It's really concerning to hear that someone who was subjected to this kind of behaviour felt that they weren't able to report what had happened to them to the police, because they lacked confidence that anything would be done about it."

summary: A 21-year-old Muslim woman named Salsabil stated she faces daily Islamophobic abuse in London, culminating in a recent incident on a bus where a man verbally abused and threatened her over her niqab. Another passenger intervened and defended her before the man was asked to leave the bus by the driver. Salsabil chose not to report the incident to the Metropolitan Police, citing previous dismissive responses from officers. Both Transport for London and the Met Police expressed concern over the videoed incident and urged witnesses to report hate crimes.
key_points: Salsabil stated she experiences Islamophobic abuse, including spitting and pushing, on a daily basis in London.
During a bus journey on 31 July, a passenger verbally abused her, accused her of terrorism, and threatened to remove her niqab and kill her.
One passenger intervened and defended Salsabil in a physical altercation before the abuser was removed from the bus.
Salsabil did not report the incident to the police because she felt previous reports were dismissed.
Transport for London and the Met Police stated they have a zero-tolerance approach to anti-Muslim hatred and are looking into the incident.
